beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Score them against a 30-claim benchmark and keep the winner.
beats.got: We test several ways of checking the AI's work and keep the best one, though I'm not sure what a claim is yet.

beats.trigger: two public-record cases with documented organisational root causes
beats.got: Real cases where the failure was a missing check in the organisation. That is a people and process question, which I like.

beats.trigger: Build a reusable judge file from the winning method that names what it catches and where it stops
beats.got: A 'judge' is a saved checker with a stated limit. I would like to know who owns it.

beats.got: I don't know which parts of an AI answer to trust, and this module is meant to help with that. That is a reputation question for me.

beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Grounded, and four candidates to measure
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: When your sources support a request, the output is grounded. When they don't, the agent still produces something, and the tone looks the same.
beats.got: The AI sounds equally sure whether it has a source or not, so I can't judge by tone.

beats.trigger: come to about 20% end-to-end: one task in five correct, four in five with a defect, usually where you won't see it.
beats.got: Small error rates multiply over a long workflow. A process with no check is far less reliable than it feels.

beats.trigger: Compounding that destroys single-pass reliability builds loop reliability.
beats.got: Checking and fixing in rounds shrinks the errors quickly. The numbers are invented, so I take it as an illustration.

beats.trigger: Fluency is not evidence, and the model cannot tell you which parts of its output are grounded.
beats.got: Asking the AI 'are you sure?' is useless. I have done exactly that myself.

beats.trigger: Run several candidate methods in parallel and measure which one catches what your benchmark says it should.
beats.got: Test the checking methods on my own material instead of trusting whoever recommends one.

beats.trigger: Catches *citation cargo-cult*.
beats.got: Four checking methods, each catching a different kind of error. That is a third technical block with no word about people, and 'entailment' came up before it was explained.

beats.trigger: You make more candidates than you need, then pick on evidence.
beats.got: The legal case shows each method catching a different mistake. It is concrete, but I'm lost on the sanctions detail.

beats.trigger: Grounded output names what it doesn't know. A grounded judge names what it can't catch.
beats.got: A good checker says what it misses. That honesty is something I could ask of any process or any person.

beats.trigger: invented case law, invented medications, confident numbers nobody can source
beats.got: Fabrication is the named failure. The medication example reminds me that it can hurt people.

beats.trigger: Stable claims can still be unsupported; drift is a warning signal, not proof of fabrication.
beats.got: Running it twice and comparing is a weak signal. I'm glad it says so.

beats.trigger: The winner becomes a judge file you carry into Module 6.
beats.got: I build the benchmark, the agents do the work, and I keep a reusable checker.

beats.trigger: Aim for roughly 10% fabrication or misrepresentation: enough wrongness for the detectors to have a job, not nonsense.
beats.got: I have the AI write a briefing with deliberate errors so the checkers have something to find. It feels odd but I follow it. I'm not sure which of my own sources it used.

beats.trigger: It runs in its own context, so your main session never sees what was fabricated.
beats.got: A separate worker writes the flawed text so my session stays blind. This is like a blind review.

beats.trigger: Thirty is not statistical, but enough to start seeing the pattern.
beats.got: The AI splits the briefing into 30 individual statements to check. I'm glad it admits 30 isn't statistical.

beats.trigger: Four helper agents run in parallel on the same claim pool, each with its own detection method and its own output file.
beats.got: I paste prompts and wait while four helpers run. I'm mostly waiting, and nothing here involves people.

beats.trigger: It measures precision (of what the detector flagged, how much was ungrounded?), recall
beats.got: Precision is how often a flag is right, and recall is how much of the real problem got caught. The explanation on my own rows helped.

beats.trigger: The scoreboard IS the explanation. You can point at a row and say *this is why I'm keeping this one*.
beats.got: I can defend my choice of checker with a table, not a feeling. That would work in a leadership meeting.

beats.trigger: The "known limit" line names what you measured and decided not to chase.
beats.got: I now have a saved checker file that states its own limits. I could show it to an HR partner.

beats.trigger: You chose by measurement, not by reputation.
beats.got: I picked by testing, and a real version needs hundreds of claims. I still haven't thought about who maintains this.

beats.trigger: The pattern (candidates → benchmark → scorer → winner) works for any quality judgment you automate.
beats.got: Candidates, benchmark, scorer, winner is a pattern I can reuse. It might work for checking people-metrics summaries.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the benchmark and updates the root instructions file with rules for when future sessions run a groundedness check
beats.got: The AI writes check-before-trust rules into a settings file. I don't know what a root instructions file is.

beats.trigger: The agent's report describes what it intended, not what is in the file.
beats.got: The AI's report says what it meant to do, not what it did, so someone has to check the file.

beats.trigger: customer names in account summaries, policy claims in internal advice
beats.got: Put a check where a miss is repeated and costly. Policy claims in internal advice is HR territory for me.

beats.trigger: Propose, double-check, apply.
beats.got: The agent proposes, a person or judge checks, then it acts. That is a clear approval pattern.

beats.trigger: The expert reviews the proposed action, the evidence behind it, and the known limit of the check that passed it.
beats.got: A human expert stays in the loop and sees what the check can't catch. That is the answer for roles and for the works council.

beats.trigger: Grounded means traceable to a source; accurate is harder.
beats.got: A recap. Traceable to a source is not the same as true.

beats.trigger: Ethan Mollick, "Garbage Can and Bitter Lesson."
beats.got: Reading for next time. I'll see whether I get to it.

beats.trigger: Evals scale it to three hundred claims, run the judge on every build, and feed its feedback into generation between rounds.
beats.got: Next is the same thing at scale and automated. I'm not sure what 'every build' means for me.

take_homes: Never trust an AI answer because it sounds sure. Fluent text is not evidence, and asking 'are you sure?' proves nothing.
Pick a quality check by testing a few options on my own material and keeping the one the scoreboard supports. Every check should state what it misses.
For anything that matters, the agent proposes, a check or an expert reviews, and only then does it act. This gives me an answer for the works council and the leadership team.

monday.move: Ask one HR business partner which repeated, costly errors in our people-metrics summaries we'd want a check on. Then try the candidates-and-scoreboard idea on one of those summaries, using non-personal sample data only.
monday.who: Me, with one HR business partner. DPO and works council first, before any real employee data goes into a tool.
monday.when: Thursday, after I've emailed the DPO
monday.stop_condition: The DPO or works council says no or wants more time, or the check can't name its own limit.
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I haven't asked yet.

misconception.why: The module was about checking output quality, not about which roles go. The human-expert-in-the-loop line made me think roles may change rather than disappear, but nobody said that and I still expect headcount questions in the leadership meeting.

one_line: Useful for learning not to trust a confident AI answer, and I liked the scoreboard idea, but it's heavy on method and says nothing about what it means for people.
